title: 15. Nikanor Ivanovich’s dream
paragraphs: It is not hard to guess that the fat man with the purple physiognomy who had been put in room No. 119 at the clinic was Nikanor Ivanovich Bosoy.
He did not, however, come to Professor Stravinsky straight away, but only after first spending some time in another place.
Of this other place Nikanor Ivanovich retained little in his memory. All he remembered was a desk, a cupboard and a sofa.

There, with Nikanor Ivanovich, whose eyes kept clouding over from rushes of blood and agitation of spirit, a conversation was begun, but the conversation came out somehow strange and muddled, or, to put it better, did not come out at all.
The very first question put to Nikanor Ivanovich was this:
“You are Nikanor Ivanovich Bosoy, chairman of the house committee at No. 302-bis on Sadovaya?”
To this Nikanor Ivanovich, laughing a terrible laugh, replied literally as follows:
“I’m Nikanor, of course I’m Nikanor! But what the deuce kind of chairman am I!”
“Meaning what?” they asked Nikanor Ivanovich, narrowing their eyes.

“Meaning this,” he answered, “that if I was a chairman, I ought to have established at once that he was the unclean power! Otherwise what is all this? Cracked pince-nez... all in rags... What kind of interpreter for a foreigner can he be!”
“Who are you talking about?” they asked Nikanor Ivanovich.
“Koroviev!” cried Nikanor Ivanovich. “He’s dug himself in at our apartment No. 50! Write it down: Koroviev. He must be caught immediately! Write it down: entrance six, that’s where he is.”
“Where did you get the foreign currency?” they asked Nikanor Ivanovich in a heart-to-heart tone.

“The true God, God almighty,” Nikanor Ivanovich began, “sees everything, and it serves me right. I never held it in my hands and never suspected what sort of thing currency was! The Lord is punishing me for my foulness,” Nikanor Ivanovich went on with feeling, now buttoning his shirt, now unbuttoning it, now crossing himself. “I took! I took, but I took ours, Soviet money! I registered people for money, I won’t argue, it happened. And our secretary Prolezhnev is a fine one too, a fine one! Let’s say it straight: they’re all thieves in the house management. But currency I never took!”

At a request to stop playing the fool and tell how the dollars had got into the ventilation shaft, Nikanor Ivanovich went down on his knees and swayed, opening his mouth as if he wished to swallow a block of the parquet.
“If you like,” he moaned, “I’ll eat dirt to prove I didn’t take it! And Koroviev—he’s the devil!”
There is a limit to all patience, and at the desk they had already raised their voices and hinted to Nikanor Ivanovich that it was time he started speaking in human language.
At this the room with that very sofa rang with a wild roar from Nikanor Ivanovich, who had jumped up from his knees:
“There he is! There he is behind the cupboard! There, he’s grinning! And his pince-nez... Hold him! Sprinkle the premises with holy water!”
The blood drained from Nikanor Ivanovich’s face; trembling, he made the sign of the cross in the air, dashed to the door and back, struck up some prayer, and at last started talking utter gibberish.
It became perfectly clear that Nikanor Ivanovich was fit for no conversation of any kind. He was led out and put in a separate room, where he calmed down somewhat and only prayed and sobbed.

They did, of course, go to Sadovaya and visit apartment No. 50. But they found no Koroviev there, and nobody in the building knew or had ever seen any Koroviev. The apartment occupied by the late Berlioz and by Likhodeyev, who had gone off to Yalta, was empty, and in the study the wax seals hung peacefully on the cupboards, undamaged by anyone. And with that they left Sadovaya, and along with those who left went the bewildered and crushed secretary of the house management, Prolezhnev.

In the evening Nikanor Ivanovich was delivered to Stravinsky’s clinic. There he behaved so restlessly that he had to be given an injection according to Stravinsky’s prescription, and only after midnight did Nikanor Ivanovich fall asleep in room 119, now and then letting out a heavy, suffering moan.
But the further it went, the lighter his sleep became. He stopped tossing and groaning, began to breathe easily and evenly, and they left him alone.

Then Nikanor Ivanovich was visited by a dream, at the root of which, undoubtedly, lay his experiences of that day. It began with Nikanor Ivanovich seeing, as it were, some people with golden trumpets in their hands leading him, and very solemnly, up to a large lacquered door. At this door his companions seemed to play a fanfare in Nikanor Ivanovich’s honor, and then a booming bass voice from the heavens said merrily:
“Welcome, Nikanor Ivanovich! Hand over your currency!”
Extremely surprised, Nikanor Ivanovich saw a black loudspeaker above him.

Then for some reason he found himself in a theater auditorium, where crystal chandeliers shone beneath a gilded ceiling, and sconces on the walls. Everything was as it ought to be, as in a theater small in size but very rich. There was a stage, closed off by a velvet curtain whose dark cherry ground was strewn, like little stars, with pictures of enlarged gold ten-rouble pieces; there was a prompter’s box, and there was even an audience.

What surprised Nikanor Ivanovich was that this whole audience was of one sex—the male—and all of them, for some reason, had beards. Besides that, it was striking that there were no chairs in the auditorium, and this whole audience was sitting on the floor, which was splendidly polished and slippery.

Embarrassed in this new and large company, Nikanor Ivanovich, after shifting about for a while, followed the general example and sat down cross-legged on the parquet, settling himself between some hefty red-bearded fellow and another, pale and very overgrown citizen. None of those sitting there paid any attention to the newly arrived spectator.

Then the soft ring of a little bell was heard, the lights in the auditorium went out, the curtain parted, and a lit stage was revealed, with an armchair, a little table on which stood a golden bell, and a solid black velvet backdrop.

At this an artiste in a dinner jacket came out from the wings, clean-shaven and with his hair parted, young and with very pleasant features. The audience in the hall livened up and everyone turned toward the stage. The artiste walked up to the prompter’s box and rubbed his hands.
“Still sitting?” he asked in a soft baritone, and smiled at the house.
“We’re sitting, we’re sitting,” the tenors and basses answered him in chorus from the hall.

“Hm...” the artiste began pensively, “and how is it you don’t get bored, I don’t understand? Everybody else, like normal people, is out walking in the streets just now, enjoying the spring sunshine and warmth, and here you are stuck on the floor in a stuffy hall! Is the program really so interesting? However, to each his own,” the artiste concluded philosophically.
Then he changed both the timbre of his voice and his intonation, and announced gaily and resonantly:
“And so, the next number on our program: Nikanor Ivanovich Bosoy, chairman of a house committee and manager of a dietary canteen. A warm welcome, please, for Nikanor Ivanovich!”

Unanimous applause was the answer to the artiste. Astonished, Nikanor Ivanovich goggled, while the master of ceremonies, shielding his eyes with his hand from the glare of the footlights, found him with his gaze among those sitting there and beckoned him tenderly onto the stage with a finger. And Nikanor Ivanovich, without knowing how, found himself on the stage. The light of colored lamps struck his eyes from below and in front, so that the hall with its audience at once sank into darkness.
“Well, now, Nikanor Ivanovich, set us an example,” the young artiste said warmly, “and hand over your currency.”
Silence fell. Nikanor Ivanovich caught his breath and began quietly:
“I swear to God that...”
But before he had got these words out, the whole hall burst into shouts of indignation. Nikanor Ivanovich lost his head and fell silent.
“As far as I understood you,” said the host of the program, “you were about to swear to God that you have no currency?” And he looked sympathetically at Nikanor Ivanovich.
“Exactly so, I haven’t,” replied Nikanor Ivanovich.

“I see,” responded the artiste, “but forgive my indiscretion: then where did the four hundred dollars come from that were found in the lavatory of the apartment whose only occupants are you and your spouse?”
“Magic dollars!” someone in the dark hall said, with obvious irony.

“Exactly so, magic,” Nikanor Ivanovich answered timidly, addressing no one in particular, whether the artiste or the dark hall, and explained: “The unclean powers, the checked interpreter, planted them on me.”
And again the hall roared with indignation. When silence fell, the artiste said:
“Just listen to the La Fontaine fables I have to put up with! Four hundred dollars planted on him! Now you here are all currency dealers, and I address you as experts: is such a thing conceivable?”
“We’re not currency dealers,” a few offended voices rang out in the theater, “but the thing is inconceivable.”
“I agree entirely,” said the artiste firmly, “and I will ask you: what can be planted on somebody, or left on a doorstep?”
“A baby!” someone shouted from the hall.

“Absolutely right,” the host of the program confirmed, “a baby, an anonymous letter, a leaflet, an infernal machine, who knows what else, but nobody is going to plant four hundred dollars on anyone, for no such idiot exists in nature.” And, turning to Nikanor Ivanovich, the artiste added reproachfully and sadly: “You’ve upset me, Nikanor Ivanovich! And I was counting on you. And so our number has not come off.”
Whistles aimed at Nikanor Ivanovich rang out in the hall.
“He’s a currency dealer!” they shouted in the hall. “It’s because of people like him that innocent folk like us have to suffer!”
“Don’t scold him,” the master of ceremonies said gently, “he will repent.” And, turning his blue eyes, full of tears, on Nikanor Ivanovich, he added: “Well, go back to your place, Nikanor Ivanovich.”
After this the artiste rang the bell and announced loudly:
“Intermission, you scoundrels!”

Shaken, Nikanor Ivanovich, who to his own surprise had become a participant in some theatrical program, found himself back in his place on the floor. Then he dreamed that the hall was plunged into total darkness and that red burning words leaped out on the walls: “Hand over your currency!” Then the curtain opened again and the master of ceremonies invited:
“Sergei Gerardovich Dunchil to the stage, please.”
Dunchil turned out to be a respectable-looking but badly neglected man of about fifty.

“Sergei Gerardovich,” the master of ceremonies addressed him, “for a month and a half now you have been sitting here, stubbornly refusing to hand over the currency you still have, while the country is in need of it and you have no use for it whatsoever, and still you persist. You are an educated man, you understand all this perfectly well, and yet you won’t meet me halfway.”
“Unfortunately, I can do nothing, since I have no more currency,” Dunchil answered calmly.
“Then haven’t you, at least, some diamonds?” asked the artiste.
“No diamonds either.”

The artiste hung his head and fell to thinking, and then clapped his hands. From the wings a middle-aged lady came out onto the stage, dressed in the fashion, that is, in a coat without a collar and a tiny hat. The lady looked alarmed, while Dunchil glanced at her without moving an eyebrow.
“Who is this lady?” the host of the program asked Dunchil.
“This is my wife,” Dunchil replied with dignity, and looked at the lady’s long neck with a certain distaste.
“We have troubled you, Madame Dunchil,” the master of ceremonies turned to the lady, “for the following reason: we wished to ask you whether your spouse has any more currency?”
“He handed it all over that time,” Madame Dunchil answered nervously.

“I see,” said the artiste, “well, then, if that is so, so be it. If he has handed it all over, then we must part with Sergei Gerardovich immediately; what can one do! If you please, you may leave the theater, Sergei Gerardovich,” and the artiste made a regal gesture.
Calmly and with dignity, Dunchil turned and walked toward the wings.
“One little minute!” the master of ceremonies stopped him. “Allow me, by way of farewell, to show you one more number from our program,” and again he clapped his hands.

The black rear curtain parted, and onto the stage came a young beauty in a ball gown, holding a little golden tray on which lay a thick bundle tied with candy-box ribbon and a diamond necklace from which blue, yellow and red fires leaped in all directions.
Dunchil took a step back and his face went pale. The hall froze.

“Eighteen thousand dollars and a necklace worth forty thousand in gold,” the artiste announced solemnly, “were kept by Sergei Gerardovich in the city of Kharkov, in the apartment of his mistress, Ida Gerkulanovna Vors, whom we have the pleasure of seeing before us, and who kindly helped to discover these treasures, priceless, yet pointless in the hands of a private person. Thank you very much, Ida Gerkulanovna.”
The beauty smiled, flashing her teeth, and her shaggy eyelashes fluttered.

“And beneath your mask of dignity,” the artiste turned to Dunchil, “there hides a greedy spider and an astounding swindler and liar. In a month and a half you have worn everyone out with your obtuse stubbornness. Go home now, and may the hell your spouse will arrange for you be your punishment.”
Dunchil swayed and seemed about to collapse, but someone’s sympathetic hands caught him. At this the front curtain came crashing down and hid all those on the stage.

Frenzied applause shook the hall so that it seemed to Nikanor Ivanovich that the lights were jumping in the chandeliers. And when the front curtain went up, there was no longer anyone on the stage except the lone artiste. He drew a second volley of applause, bowed, and began to speak:

“In the person of this Dunchil, you have seen a typical ass perform in our program. After all, I had the pleasure of saying yesterday that the secret hoarding of currency is nonsense. Nobody can make use of it under any circumstances, I assure you. Take this Dunchil, for instance. He receives a splendid salary and wants for nothing. He has a fine apartment, a wife and a beautiful mistress. But no! Instead of living quietly and peacefully, without any unpleasantness, by handing over the currency and the stones, this mercenary blockhead got himself exposed in front of everyone after all, and for dessert acquired the biggest of family troubles. And so, who will hand over? Nobody willing? In that case, the next number on our program: that celebrated dramatic talent, the artiste Savva Potapovich Kurolesov, especially invited, will perform excerpts from The Covetous Knight by the poet Pushkin.”
The promised Kurolesov was not slow to appear on the stage and turned out to be a tall, fleshy, clean-shaven man in tails and a white tie.
Without any preamble he put on a gloomy face, knitted his brows and began to speak in an unnatural voice, glancing sidelong at the golden bell:
“As a young rake awaits his assignation with some sly harlot of depraved desire...”

And Kurolesov told a great many bad things about himself. Nikanor Ivanovich heard Kurolesov confess that some unhappy widow, howling, had knelt before him in the rain but had not touched the artiste’s callous heart.

Before his dream Nikanor Ivanovich had known absolutely nothing of the works of the poet Pushkin, but he knew the man himself perfectly well, and several times a day he would utter phrases like: “And is Pushkin going to pay the rent, then?” or “So it was Pushkin who unscrewed the light bulb on the stairs, was it?” or “So Pushkin’s going to buy the fuel oil, is he?”

Now, having become acquainted with one of his works, Nikanor Ivanovich grew sad, pictured to himself the woman on her knees, with orphans, in the rain, and could not help thinking: “What a character that Kurolesov is, though!”

And he, raising his voice all the while, went on repenting and thoroughly confused Nikanor Ivanovich, because he suddenly began addressing someone who was not on the stage, and answered himself on behalf of this absent person, calling himself now “sovereign,” now “baron,” now “father,” now “son,” now with the formal “you,” now with the familiar one.
Nikanor Ivanovich understood only one thing: that the artiste died an evil death, crying out, “The keys! My keys!” and collapsing on the floor after this, wheezing and carefully tearing off his tie.
Having died, Kurolesov got up, brushed the dust off his tailcoat trousers, bowed, smiling a false smile, and withdrew to thin applause. And the master of ceremonies said this:

“We have just heard The Covetous Knight in the remarkable performance of Savva Potapovich. This knight hoped that sportive nymphs would come running to him, and that a great many more pleasant things in the same vein would happen. But, as you see, none of this occurred: no nymphs came running to him, and the muses brought him no tribute, and he raised no palaces of any kind, but, on the contrary, ended very badly—he dropped dead—to the devil with him—of a stroke on his chest full of currency and stones. I warn you that something of the kind will happen to you too, if not worse, if you don’t hand over your currency!”
Whether it was Pushkin’s poetry that made such an impression or the prosaic speech of the master of ceremonies, but suddenly a shy voice rang out from the hall:
“I’ll hand over my currency.”
“Be so kind as to come up on the stage,” the master of ceremonies invited politely, peering into the dark hall.
And on the stage appeared a short, fair-haired citizen who, judging by his face, had not shaved for about three weeks.
“Excuse me, what is your name?” the master of ceremonies inquired.
“Kanavkin, Nikolai,” the newcomer responded shyly.
“Ah! A pleasure, citizen Kanavkin. Well?”
“I’ll hand it over,” Kanavkin said quietly.
“How much?”
“A thousand dollars and twenty gold ten-rouble pieces.”
“Bravo! Is that all you have?”

The host of the program stared straight into Kanavkin’s eyes, and it even seemed to Nikanor Ivanovich that rays spurted from those eyes and pierced Kanavkin right through, like X-rays. The hall stopped breathing.

“I believe you!” the artiste exclaimed at last, and extinguished his gaze. “I believe you! These eyes do not lie. How many times have I told you that your basic mistake is that you underestimate the significance of human eyes. Understand that the tongue can conceal the truth, but the eyes—never! You are asked a sudden question, you don’t even flinch, in one second you take control of yourself and know what must be said to hide the truth, and you say it very convincingly, and not a single fold of your face stirs, but, alas, the truth, alarmed by the question, leaps for an instant from the bottom of your soul into your eyes, and it’s all over. It has been noticed, and you are caught!”
Having delivered, and with great fervor, this very convincing speech, the artiste tenderly inquired of Kanavkin:
“And where are they hidden?”
“At my aunt’s, Porokhovnikova’s, on Prechistenka...”
“Ah! That’s... wait... that’s Klavdia Ilyinichna’s, isn’t it?”
“Yes.”
“Ah, yes, yes, yes, yes! The little private house? With the little front garden opposite? Of course, I know it, I know it! And where did you stick them there?”
“In the cellar, in an Einem chocolate box...”
The artiste threw up his hands.

“Have you ever seen anything like it?” he cried in distress. “Why, they’ll go moldy there, they’ll get damp! Well, is it conceivable to entrust currency to such people? Eh? Just like children, honest to God!”
Kanavkin himself understood that he had blundered and put his foot in it, and hung his tufted head.

“Money,” the artiste went on, “ought to be kept in the State Bank, in special dry and well-guarded premises, and certainly not in an aunt’s cellar, where, in particular, the rats may damage it! Really, you ought to be ashamed, Kanavkin! You’re a grown man, after all.”
Kanavkin no longer knew where to put himself and only picked at the lapel of his jacket with his finger.

“Well, all right,” the artiste relented, “let bygones be bygones...” And suddenly he added unexpectedly: “Oh, by the way... so as to do it all in one go... so as not to send the car out for nothing... this same aunt has some too, hasn’t she, eh?”
Kanavkin, who had in no way expected such a turn of events, flinched, and silence fell in the theater.

“Eh, Kanavkin,” the master of ceremonies said with tender reproach, “and here I was praising him! And there you go, he’s gone and stumbled out of the blue! It’s absurd, Kanavkin! I was only just talking about the eyes. Anyone can see the aunt has some. Well, why do you torment us for nothing?”
“She has!” Kanavkin cried recklessly.
“Bravo!” cried the master of ceremonies.
“Bravo!” the hall roared terribly.

When things had quieted down, the master of ceremonies congratulated Kanavkin, shook his hand, offered to have him driven home to town in a car, and ordered someone in the wings to call by for the aunt in that same car and ask her to kindly attend a program at the women’s theater.

“Oh yes, I wanted to ask: didn’t your aunt say where she hides her own?” the master of ceremonies inquired, courteously offering Kanavkin a cigarette and a lighted match. Lighting up, the latter gave a rather dreary smirk.

“I believe you, I believe you,” the artiste responded with a sigh. “That old skinflint wouldn’t tell it to the devil, let alone her nephew. Well, then, we shall try to awaken human feelings in her. Perhaps not all the strings have rotted yet in her little usurer’s soul. All the best, Kanavkin!”
And the happy Kanavkin drove off. The artiste inquired whether there was anyone else who wished to hand over currency, but received silence in reply.
“Odd fellows, honest to God!” said the artiste with a shrug, and the curtain hid him.
The lamps went out, for a while there was darkness, and from far off in it could be heard a nervous tenor singing:
“There heaps of gold lie shining bright, and all of them are mine by right!”
Then, from somewhere, applause came faintly twice.

“Some little lady is handing hers over in the women’s theater,” Nikanor Ivanovich’s red-bearded neighbor suddenly spoke up, and with a sigh he added: “Eh, if it weren’t for my geese!.. I’ve got fighting geese, my dear man, in Lianozovo... They’ll die without me, I’m afraid. A fighting bird, delicate, needs looking after... Eh, if it weren’t for the geese! You won’t surprise me with Pushkin,” and he started sighing again.

Here the hall lit up brightly, and Nikanor Ivanovich began dreaming that cooks in white hats and with ladles in their hands came pouring into the hall from all the doors. Kitchen boys dragged into the hall a vat of soup and a tray of sliced black bread. The spectators livened up. The merry cooks darted among the theatergoers, ladled soup into bowls and handed out bread.

“Eat your dinner, lads,” the cooks shouted, “and hand over your currency! Why sit here for nothing? Who’d want to slurp this swill! Go home, have a proper drink, a bite to go with it—that’s the life!”

“Now why, for instance, have you dug yourself in here, old fellow?” a fat cook with a raspberry-colored neck addressed Nikanor Ivanovich directly, holding out to him a bowl in which a single cabbage leaf floated in liquid.
“I haven’t got any! I haven’t! I haven’t got any!” Nikanor Ivanovich shouted in a terrible voice. “Understand, I haven’t!”
“You haven’t?” the cook roared in a menacing bass. “You haven’t?” he asked in a tender woman’s voice. “You haven’t, you haven’t,” he muttered soothingly, turning into the nurse Praskovya Fyodorovna.

She was gently shaking Nikanor Ivanovich by the shoulder as he moaned in his sleep. Then the cooks melted away, and the theater with its curtain fell to pieces. Through his tears Nikanor Ivanovich made out his room in the hospital and two people in white coats, though by no means the cheeky cooks who poke their noses into people’s business with their advice, but the doctor and that same Praskovya Fyodorovna, holding in her hands not a bowl but a little dish covered with gauze, with a syringe lying on it.
“What is all this?” Nikanor Ivanovich said bitterly while they gave him the injection. “I haven’t got any, and that’s that! Let Pushkin hand over currency to them. I haven’t got any!”
“No, you haven’t, you haven’t,” the kind-hearted Praskovya Fyodorovna soothed him, “and where there’s none, there’s no case to answer.”
Nikanor Ivanovich felt better after the injection, and he fell asleep without any dreams at all.

But thanks to his shouts the alarm spread to room 120, where the patient woke up and began looking for his head, and to room 118, where the unknown master grew restless and wrung his hands in anguish, looking at the moon, remembering the bitter last autumn night of his life, the strip of light under the door in the basement, and the hair come loose from its curls.
From room 118 the alarm flew along the balcony to Ivan, and he woke up and wept.

But the doctor quickly calmed all the alarmed, those afflicted in the head, and they began to fall asleep. Ivan was the last of all to drift off, when it was already growing light over the river. After the medicine, which soaked into his whole body, calm came to him like a wave that covered him. His body grew lighter, and drowsiness fanned his head with a warm breeze. He fell asleep, and the last thing he heard while awake was the predawn twittering of birds in the forest. But they soon fell silent, and he began dreaming that the sun was already descending over Bald Mountain, and this mountain was cordoned off by a double cordon...
